```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE,
                     fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 110)
library(LHWL)
```

## What this guide covers

This companion to the [introduction](lorentz-hgwr-introduction.html)
explains the decisions between supplying coordinates and reporting a fitted
Gaussian LHWR model. The [graphics gallery](lhwr-graphics.html) shows how to
display the resulting quantities. The separate [Lasso guide](lhwpr-lasso.html)
covers penalized tuning: its active sets and selection criteria must not be
confused with unpenalized coefficient inference.

All examples are small, offline documentation checks, not a new empirical
study. They reuse the introduction's 141-country WDI 2024 sample, response,
standardized regressors, stored representation and five-candidate grid.
No observations are removed or imputed. Standardization below applies to
the two regression predictors, not to the supplied Lorentz coordinates.

```{r analysis-data}
data("wdi_lhwr")
wdi <- subset(wdi_lhwr, year == 2024)
Z <- as.matrix(wdi[, c("z0_lorentz", "z1_lorentz", "z2_lorentz")])
dat <- data.frame(gdp_growth = wdi$gdp_growth,
  unemployment = as.numeric(scale(wdi$unemployment)),
  internet_users = as.numeric(scale(wdi$internet_users)))
form <- gdp_growth ~ unemployment + internet_users
candidate_k <- seq(30, 70, by = 10)
stopifnot(nrow(dat) == 141L, !anyNA(dat), nrow(Z) == nrow(dat))
```

## Kernel shape is different from bandwidth

Let \(d_{ij}\geq0\) be the chosen distance between observations \(i\) and
\(j\), and \(h_i>0\) a local distance radius. Kernel weights are
\(w_{ij}=K(u_{ij})\), where \(u_{ij}=d_{ij}/h_i\) is dimensionless.
The kernel sets how quickly influence decays with relative distance;
the radius sets the scale of the neighbourhood. The five implemented
functions are shown below for \(u\geq0\). Compact kernels are **zero at**
\(u=1\), not only outside the radius.

```{r kernel-definitions, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Kernel = c("bisquare", "tricube", "boxcar", "gaussian", "exponential"),
  `K(u)` = c("(1-u^2)^2 for u<1; 0 otherwise",
             "(1-u^3)^3 for u<1; 0 otherwise",
             "1 for u<1; 0 otherwise", "exp(-u^2/2)", "exp(-u)"),
  Support = c(rep("Compact", 3), rep("Noncompact", 2)), check.names = FALSE
), caption = "Implemented kernel formulas for nonnegative relative distance.")
```

```{r kernel-curves, fig.cap="Kernel weights versus distance divided by bandwidth. Gaussian and exponential weights remain positive beyond the radius; the three compact kernels have zero boundary weight."}
kernel_names <- c("bisquare", "tricube", "boxcar", "gaussian", "exponential")
u <- seq(0, 3, length.out = 301)
kernel_weights <- sapply(kernel_names, function(k) hgwr_kernel(u, 1, k))
kernel_cols <- c("#176B72", "#7B3294", "#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#6B6B00")
matplot(u, kernel_weights, type = "l", lty = seq_along(kernel_names),
        col = kernel_cols, lwd = 2, xlab = "Relative distance d / h",
        ylab = "Kernel weight", ylim = c(0, 1.05))
abline(v = 1, lty = 3, col = "grey65")
legend("topright", kernel_names, col = kernel_cols,
       lty = seq_along(kernel_names), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

Changing a kernel changes the estimator. Comparing kernels requires the
same analysis sample, representation and a declared selection protocol;
these curves do not establish that one kernel is best. Do not truncate a
Gaussian or exponential kernel merely to obtain a faster computation.

## What `bw`, `adaptive` and `engine` mean

```{r bandwidth-contract, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Setting = c("adaptive=TRUE, bandwidth_type='knn'",
              "adaptive=FALSE, bandwidth_type='knn'",
              "adaptive=FALSE, bandwidth_type='volume'",
              "adaptive=TRUE, bandwidth_type='volume'"),
  `Meaning of scalar bw` = c("Target positive-distance neighbour rank k",
    "Fixed distance radius h", "Fixed hyperbolic ball area V",
    "Target local mass; radius obtained using a pilot density"),
  Engine = c("dense or supported knn", rep("dense", 3)), check.names = FALSE
), caption = "Bandwidth contracts. Volume options require Lorentz geometry.")
```

For adaptive kNN bandwidths, the radius is the distance to the requested
positive-distance neighbour rank. The focal observation has zero distance
and is used in calibration, but does not count toward that positive-distance
rank. Coincident points and boundary ties make `bw` different from the count
of strictly positive regression weights. Inspect `local_n_positive` and
`local_neff` rather than reporting `bw` as an effective sample size.

For the two-dimensional unit-curvature model, ball area and its inverse are
\(V(h)=2\pi(\cosh h-1)\) and
\(h(V)=\operatorname{arcosh}\{1+V/(2\pi)\}\), for \(h,V\geq0\).
These convert between intrinsic radius and area. In adaptive-volume mode,
`pilot_k` supplies the pilot neighbour rank used to estimate local point
density; target mass divided by that density gives a target area, which is
then inverted. This is a different bandwidth rule, not another name for kNN.

The **kNN engine** is a computational choice: exact Lorentz neighbours with
adaptive kNN bandwidths and `bisquare`, `tricube` or `boxcar` kernels. It does
not support tangent geometry, supplied `dMat`, fixed radii, volume bandwidths,
Gaussian or exponential kernels. Use `engine="dense"` for those cases.
The dense engine stores an \(n\)-by-\(n\) distance matrix; kNN reduces that
storage, but some post-fit diagnostics still reconstruct dense operators.
`n_threads=1` is the reproducible serial default, not a statistical parameter.

## AICc and CV select a bandwidth; AIC and BIC summarize a fit

For a Gaussian LHWR fit, let \(n\) be the sample size, \(S\) its conditional
smoother matrix such that \(\widehat y=Sy\), and
\(R=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2>0\) its residual sum of squares.
Define \(t=\operatorname{tr}(S)\), the smoother trace. The implementation
uses the Gaussian deviance-like quantity
\(D=n\log(R/n)+n\log(2\pi)+n\) and the following information criteria:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AIC}&=D+2(t+1),\\
\mathrm{AICc}&=D+\frac{2n(t+1)}{n-t-2},\\
\mathrm{BIC}&=D+\log(n)(t+1).
\end{aligned}\tag{1}
\]

Equation (1) balances calibration fit and conditional model complexity;
the extra one accounts for the variance parameter. AICc requires
\(n-t-2>0\); the package assigns an infinite score otherwise. The trace is
not the number of predictors. These working smoother criteria do not add a
penalty for learning the representation or searching over representations.
Scores are comparable only under a common response, sample and likelihood
convention; a smaller score is not a hypothesis-test p-value.

Gaussian CV instead evaluates
\(\mathrm{CV}(b)=\sum_i\{y_i-\widehat y_{i,b}^{(-i)}\}^2\), where
\(b\) is a candidate bandwidth and \(\widehat y_{i,b}^{(-i)}\) omits
observation \(i\)'s response from its local calibration. This is a **sum**
of squared errors. The supplied coordinates and candidate neighbourhood
radii remain fixed during this internal score. It is not an outer validation
of an embedding-plus-tuning pipeline and does not reselect bandwidth inside
each held-out case. Binary-response CV uses Bernoulli log loss instead;
Gaussian AICc and F diagnostics are not defined for binomial fits.

```{r select-bandwidths}
bw_aicc <- bw.lhwr(form, dat, Z = Z, bw_grid = candidate_k,
                   approach = "AICc", kernel = "bisquare", engine = "knn")
bw_cv <- bw.lhwr(form, dat, Z = Z, bw_grid = candidate_k,
                 approach = "CV", kernel = "bisquare", engine = "knn")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Criterion = c("AICc", "CV"),
  Selected_k = c(bw_aicc$bw, bw_cv$bw),
  Score = c(bw_aicc$score, bw_cv$score)), digits = 3,
  caption = "Two criteria applied to exactly the same five candidates.")
```

```{r tuning-curves, fig.show='hold', out.width='49%', fig.width=5.2, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Left: AICc. Right: leave-one-out squared-error CV over the same neighbour counts. Vertical scales differ because the criteria have different units."}
plot_lhwr_diagnostics(bw_aicc, type = "bandwidth")
plot_lhwr_diagnostics(bw_cv, type = "bandwidth")
```

`bw.lhwr()` accepts `approach="AICc"` or `"CV"`, **not** `"AIC"` or
`"BIC"`. AIC and BIC can be extracted after fitting. An explicit `bw_grid`
selects grid search; otherwise the default is golden-section search over
an interval controlled by `lower`, `upper`, `tol` and `max_iter`.
The selected minimum is among evaluated candidates, not proof of a global
minimum over every possible bandwidth. Boundary selections warrant review
of support and search range, not automatic widening until a desired result
appears. `selection.table` records the evaluated candidates and scores.

```{r fitted-diagnostics}
fit <- lhwr(form, dat, Z = Z, bw = bw_aicc$bw, kernel = "bisquare",
            engine = "knn", diagnostics = "full", f_tests = FALSE)
diag_fit <- fit$LHWR.diagnostic
knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = c("RSS", "AIC", "AICc", "BIC", "tr(S)", "edf"),
  Value = unlist(diag_fit[c("RSS.gw", "AIC", "AICc", "BIC", "tr.S", "edf")])),
  digits = 3, caption = "Post-fit Gaussian diagnostics from the AICc-selected fit.")
CV.lhwr(bw_cv)
```

`CV.lhwr(fit)` may return `NA` when no CV score was computed for that object;
it does not start a new cross-validation. Likewise `diagnostics="none"`
does not contain the hat-matrix quantities needed for AICc or F tests.
`diagnostics="aicc"` computes trace-based summaries but omits local standard
errors; `"full"` supplies the local inference quantities used below.

## Local design and coefficient uncertainty

For weights \(w_{ij}\), effective local support is
\(n_{\mathrm{eff},i}=(\sum_j w_{ij})^2/\sum_j w_{ij}^2\), provided the
denominator is positive. It reflects uneven influence, not an independent
sample size that makes local observations exchangeable. Condition numbers,
weighted local VIFs and rank diagnostics address estimability. They do not
test whether a representation is intrinsically hyperbolic.

```{r support-and-inference}
lc <- local_collinearity(fit)
inf <- local_inference(fit, alpha = 0.05, df = "edf",
                       adjust = "BH", adjust_scope = "coefficient")
knitr::kable(head(lc$condition_number), digits = 3,
             caption = "Local design diagnostics for the first observations.")
knitr::kable(head(inf$local[, c("observation_id", "coefficient", "estimate",
                               "se", "t_value", "p_value", "p_adjusted")]),
             digits = 3, caption = "Conditional exploratory local coefficient tests.")
```

Here a local t-value is the coefficient estimate divided by its standard
error. `df="edf"` uses
\(n-2\operatorname{tr}(S)+\operatorname{tr}(S^\top S)\);
`df="residual"` uses \(n-\operatorname{tr}(S)\), while `"normal"` uses
a normal reference. These are distinct conventions, not interchangeable
labels. `adjust_scope="coefficient"` adjusts across locations separately
for each coefficient; `"global"` adjusts across all location-coefficient
pairs. Neither choice accounts for selecting the bandwidth or estimating
the representation. Multiplicity adjustment alone does not establish
valid post-selection inference or false-discovery control here.

## Conditional F1, F2 and F3 diagnostics

`diagnostic_tests()` implements Leung-type moment-matched diagnostics
(Leung, Mei and Zhang, 2000), using the LHWR smoother rather than geographic
weights. They are not the usual exact nested-model `anova()` F tests.
For fixed coordinates, weights and bandwidth, define
\(R_H=(I_n-S)^\top(I_n-S)\), where \(I_n\) is the identity matrix,
\(\delta_1=\operatorname{tr}(R_H)\) and
\(\delta_2=\operatorname{tr}(R_H^2)\).
Let \(R_0\) be the OLS RSS on the same response and model matrix, with
\(\nu_0=n-p\), where \(p\) includes the intercept. The two global statistics are

\[
F_1=\frac{R/\delta_1}{R_0/\nu_0},\qquad
F_2=\frac{(R_0-R)/\eta_1}{R_0/\nu_0},\qquad
\eta_1=\nu_0-\delta_1,\quad
\eta_2=\nu_0-2\delta_1+\delta_2.\tag{2}
\]

Equation (2) contrasts local and global residual variation. F1 uses a
**lower-tail** F reference with degrees of freedom
\((\delta_1^2/\delta_2,\nu_0)\); F2 uses an **upper-tail** reference with
\((\eta_1^2/\eta_2,\nu_0)\). A negative RSS improvement is not evidence
for locality. Required variances, moments and reference degrees of freedom
must be positive; an undefined p-value must not be replaced with zero.

F3 asks a different question: whether a particular coefficient is constant
over the representation. For coefficient \(j\), let \(B_jy\) collect its
\(n\) local estimates, \(C_0=I_n-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/n\) be the centring
matrix, and \(C_j=B_j^\top C_0B_j/n\). Here \(\mathbf1\) is the vector of
ones. Define \(\gamma_{1j}=\operatorname{tr}(C_j)\),
\(\gamma_{2j}=\operatorname{tr}(C_j^2)\) and
\(V_j^2=y^\top C_jy\), the spatial variance of the coefficient estimates.
Then the coefficient-specific statistic is

\[
F_{3,j}=\frac{V_j^2/\gamma_{1j}}{R/\delta_1}.\tag{3}
\]

Equation (3) compares coefficient variation with residual noise, using an
upper-tail reference with degrees of freedom
\((\gamma_{1j}^2/\gamma_{2j},\delta_1^2/\delta_2)\).
It tests a working **constancy** hypothesis, not whether the coefficient is
zero at one location. The reference laws are approximate: their quadratic
forms are generally dependent. Stationary coefficients and independent
homoskedastic Gaussian errors motivate them; response-selected bandwidths,
correlated errors and varying nuisance coefficients limit calibration.

```{r f-tests}
ft <- diagnostic_tests(fit)
knitr::kable(ft$global_tests, digits = 4,
             caption = "Conditional global F diagnostics, with moment-based degrees of freedom.")
knitr::kable(ft$coefficient_tests, digits = 4,
             caption = "F3 diagnostics for coefficient constancy, not pointwise nonzero effects.")
```

Alternatively request `f_tests=TRUE` during `lhwr()` and read `$Ftests`.
The default is `FALSE` because reconstructing coefficient operators can
be costly. The fitted Gaussian model must have hat-matrix diagnostics.
By default the stored OLS model ensures the same formula and observations;
if supplying `ols_model`, verify its response, design columns and row order,
not just its row count. `engine="cpp"` and the small-data reference
`engine="R"` concern diagnostic computation, not bandwidth selection.

## Global Moran and local LISA are residual diagnostics

Diagnostic weights \(W=(w_{ij}^{(H)})\) are a separate, declared choice.
They have zero diagonal, so a residual is not its own neighbour. With
`row_standardize=TRUE`, each nonempty row sums to one. These are economic
representation neighbourhoods in this example, not geographic adjacency.
Do not assume the defaults automatically reproduce a nondefault fit's
kernel, geometry or fixed/volume bandwidth rule: supply settings explicitly.

For residuals \(e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i\), define their mean \(\bar e\),
centred values \(z_i=e_i-\bar e\), \(m_2=n^{-1}\sum_i z_i^2\), and
\(S_0=\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}^{(H)}\). Moran's global statistic and the local
indicators (Moran, 1950; Anselin, 1995) are

\[
I_H=\frac{n}{S_0}\frac{\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}^{(H)}z_i z_j}{\sum_i z_i^2},
\qquad I_i^{(H)}=\frac{z_i\sum_jw_{ij}^{(H)}z_j}{m_2}.\tag{4}
\]

Equation (4) requires nonconstant residuals and positive total weight.
Global Moran summarizes association over the whole sample. LISA localizes
it: high--high and low--low are concordant residual patterns; high--low and
low--high are discordant residual outliers. High and low refer to the signs
of the **centred residual** and its weighted lag, not the response level or
the sign of a coefficient. Local indicators need not reproduce the conclusion
of a global test.

```{r residual-diagnostics}
permutations <- 99L
permutation_seed <- 20260714L
mi <- moran.lhwr(fit, distance = "lorentz", kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE, k = bw_aicc$bw, row_standardize = TRUE,
  permutations = permutations, seed = permutation_seed)
lisa <- local_moran.lhwr(fit, distance = "lorentz", kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE, k = bw_aicc$bw, row_standardize = TRUE,
  permutations = permutations, seed = permutation_seed)
knitr::kable(data.frame(I = mi$I, Expected_under_permutation = mi$expected_I,
  Raw_p = mi$p_value, Permutations = mi$permutations), digits = 4,
  caption = "Global residual association under the specified diagnostic weights.")
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(lisa$cluster_type)),
  col.names = c("Raw local classification", "Count"),
  caption = "LISA labels using the package's raw p <= 0.05 classification.")
```

The implementation permutes the **entire** centred residual vector for LISA;
it does not hold the focal residual fixed as in conditional local randomization.
Two-sided absolute deviations are measured from the permutation mean for
each local statistic, and from \(-1/(n-1)\) for global Moran. This global
expectation assumes uniform permutations of a fixed nonconstant vector and
fixed zero-diagonal weights; it is not the sampling expectation of fitted
LHWR residuals. P-values use a plus-one correction, giving increments of
\(1/(B+1)\) with \(B\) permutations. The 99-permutation example is coarse
and retained for a quick, reproducible tutorial; it is not a universal
precision recommendation. `permutations=0` returns statistics without
permutation p-values. Record the seed separately: the local result does not
store every permutation setting as metadata.

`cluster_type` uses raw `p_value <= 0.05`. Changing `alpha` in `plot(lisa)`
only masks points when `significant_only=TRUE`; it does not recalculate the
stored classes or apply a multiple-testing adjustment. The gallery shows an
explicit reclassification for a different display rule. Unflagged means
not flagged by that rule, not proven independence. A significant residual
statistic indicates remaining structure, not improved fitting by itself.

### Explicit weights and nondefault kernels

The Moran/LISA `kernel` argument directly accepts bisquare, Gaussian and
exponential. The regression functions accept five kernels. To use tricube
or boxcar diagnostically, or to make the weight definition fully explicit,
pass `W`. For example, the following reconstructs the current bisquare
diagnostic using the calibrated radii and verifies agreement:

```{r explicit-diagnostic-weights}
D <- hyperbolic_distance_matrix(Z, check = FALSE)
W <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(Z)), function(i) {
  hgwr_kernel(D[i, ], fit$bandwidth[i], kernel = "bisquare")
}, numeric(nrow(Z))))
diag(W) <- 0
stopifnot(all(rowSums(W) > 0))
W <- W / rowSums(W)
mi_explicit <- moran.lhwr(fit, W = W, permutations = 0)
stopifnot(abs(mi_explicit$I - mi$I) < 1e-10)
```

Changing the kernel in this construction is a diagnostic sensitivity analysis,
not a refit. Preserve the original diagnostic and report the changed weights.
When `W` is supplied, the matrix determines the weights; record its actual
construction rather than interpreting the function's default distance/kernel
labels as provenance. Validate its size, finite nonnegative values, row order,
diagonal and isolated rows before calling the diagnostics.

Stored kNN lists are reused only for compact bisquare diagnostic weights.
For Gaussian and exponential diagnostics, the adaptive k-neighbour radius
still defines the bandwidth, but weights are evaluated over the full distance
matrix: nonzero tails are not truncated. This requires quadratic memory in
the sample size. An explicitly constructed **full** `W` remains useful for
auditable sensitivity checks. Bisquare diagnostics are unchanged; correcting
the noncompact path does not revise any stored historical analysis.

## Reporting checklist

Report the response, predictors and units; coordinate construction and row
alignment; geometry, kernel and bandwidth rule; evaluated candidates and
selection criterion; diagnostic detail and local support; F reference and
local adjustment conventions; residual weight matrix, permutations and seed;
and software version. Keep calibration, conditional diagnostics and independent
predictive evaluation distinct. None of these diagnostics alone establishes
causality, validates a learned representation or guarantees that LHWR must
outperform a global model.

```{r session}
packageVersion("LHWL")
```

*Environment and Planning A*, 32(1), 9--32.

Moran, P. A. P. (1950). Notes on continuous stochastic phenomena.
*Biometrika*, 37(1/2), 17--23.
